display: Fashion-design lecturer in Manchester who runs a sustainable dye lab and grows woad and madder on an allotment. My funded natural-dye project is stuck because batches never come out the same twice, and the part-time technician post is unfilled.

signals.text: I've run fourteen woad vats since March with the same recipe, and the blues range from pale duck-egg to deep indigo. I can't explain the pattern.
Madder reds drift from batch to batch as well. Two kids dyeing socks in the same pot at the same time got orange-pink and brick red.
I log temperature, pH, plant age, water hardness and fermentation time, and still can't predict the colour. I suspect I'm missing a way of looking at the data, not more data.
I need a part-time technician who understands both plant dyes and process control. Chemists who've never touched a plant and dyers who've never kept a log have both come up short.
The spectrophotometer says my batches differ by delta-E 8 to 15. The instrument is fine, so the variation is in the vat.
I'm reading about CIELAB drift and want a sound way to make my batches comparable.
I'd love to talk to someone who remembers how old dye-house colour matchers corrected a shade by eye, with no machine.
Any technician hire has to start by early January, so I have a hiring clock running.
A funder mid-term review is coming up and I'd like to show real progress on reproducibility, even if the progress is a better question.
My third-year students are being assessed on matching swatches in a collection about variation. They're working with local plant colour, so it's an ironic brief.
The Slow Colour student show is on 12 December, and the students could use dye-literate people to talk to or to host them.
Students learn colour best when they dig madder at the allotment. I'd like more ways to get them outdoors and into the soil.
I'm training for a fell race in the Peak District and would be glad of running company or advice for the climbs.
The allotment woad has gone to seed. I'm saving seed and the last harvest is in early November.
I'm stretched across teaching, research, family and the repair café, and it's hard to find time to think about the vat problem properly.

offers.text: A dye lab with eight stainless-steel pots, a fume cupboard, and a pH and temperature logging setup. I can host a trial or a visit.
Fourteen-plus vats of logged woad and madder data (pH, temperature, plant age, water hardness, fermentation time) that I'm willing to share for analysis.
Practical knowledge of growing woad, madder, weld and dyer's chamomile, and of turning them into colour.
A natural-dye research project with a part-time technician post I can offer to the right person.
Access to a university spectrophotometer, shared and booked about two weeks ahead, for colour measurement collaborations.
Teaching experience in fashion design and the ability to explain colour and sustainability to students and non-specialists.
Knitwear repair and darning, including visible, memorial repairs that don't try to hide the damage.
A network of knitters and weavers through a Chorlton repair café and a Northern Quarter yarn shop.
A supply of second-best fleece from a Derbyshire farmer, traded for dyed samples.
Allotment days where visitors can dig madder or harvest woad in season.

catchers.hypo: I'm a dyer with a few years' experience and I've been keeping detailed batch logs for years. I'd like a part-time lab role where the logs actually matter.
catchers.can: Hannah can discuss the part-time technician post and arrange a lab visit.
catchers.confirm: Have you dyed with plant materials (not only synthetic or mordant dyes) and kept batch-by-batch records yourself?

catchers.hypo: I'm a process or analytical chemist who has never dyed, but I'd like to learn plants and run the controls. Is there a technician post for me?
catchers.can: Hannah can talk to them about whether they'd pair well with the dye knowledge she already has.
catchers.confirm: Are you willing to learn hands-on plant dyeing, and can you work part time on site in Manchester?

catchers.hypo: I'm a statistician with experience in design of experiments, and I enjoy messy biological data. Would you share your vat logs?
catchers.can: Hannah can share anonymised logs and discuss what variables might be confounded.
catchers.confirm: Have you analysed noisy natural-process data (fermentation, agriculture, food or similar), and not only industrial data?

catchers.hypo: I work in colour science and know CIELAB drift well. Could I help you make plant-dye batches comparable?
catchers.can: Hannah can talk through her delta-E results and what she measures.
catchers.confirm: Have you worked with spectrophotometer data from textiles or other variable organic materials?

catchers.hypo: My mother worked in a dye house, or I'm a retired colour matcher. I remember how shades were corrected by eye.
catchers.can: Hannah would be glad to interview them and record how they corrected colour.
catchers.confirm: Did you or someone you know do hands-on colour matching, adjusting a dye bath by eye?

catchers.hypo: I run a small fashion label and want plant-dyed colour I can reorder and repeat. What's realistic?
catchers.can: Hannah can tell them what current research shows about repeatability and where it breaks down.
catchers.confirm: Do you work in small batches and care about plant dyes specifically, not simply 'eco-friendly' dyes?

catchers.hypo: My small studio or charity needs a plain-spoken person to look at its basic IT and data security. Do you know anyone?
catchers.can: Hannah can ask Rob, her husband, who works in IT security, whether he can recommend someone or give a short steer.
catchers.confirm: Is this a small organisation that needs practical, basic advice and not a full security audit?

catchers.hypo: I've just lost someone and I have their knitted jumper with a moth hole. Can it be repaired?
catchers.can: Hannah can do a visible, respectful repair at the Saturday repair café, or point to someone local.
catchers.confirm: Is it a knitted or darned garment that you can bring in person on a Saturday morning in Manchester?

catchers.hypo: I teach textiles and want my students to see real plant dyeing. Could we visit the allotment or dye lab?
catchers.can: Hannah can host a limited visit, depending on season and school-run days.
catchers.confirm: Is it an educational group that can come on a day other than Wednesday and outside school holidays?

catchers.hypo: I grow dye plants or keep sheep and wonder whether anyone uses the fleece or the harvest.
catchers.can: Hannah can swap dyed samples for fleece or exchange growing knowledge, and can introduce them to her Derbyshire farmer.
catchers.confirm: Do you grow dye plants or keep sheep in the Manchester/Derbyshire area?

forbids.text: I won't work on Wednesdays because of the school run.
I can't travel during school holidays.
The project stays natural-only. I won't use synthetic dyes for it, and I won't call synthetics sustainable.
The allotment is seasonal and tied to light and weather, so I can't promise year-round field work.

projects.name: Woad & Madder Reproducibility project
projects.text: A two-year funded study to make plant dyes repeatable enough for small-batch fashion labels. It is stuck on batch-to-batch variation.
roles_needed: Part-time dye technician with process-control habits
Retired colour matcher or dye-house historian

projects.name: Slow Colour student show
projects.text: A capsule collection by seven third-year students, dyed only with plants grown within thirty miles, shown on 12 December.
roles_needed: Guest critic or speaker on natural dye

policy.t1: Teaching, the repair café, running and the Slow Colour show; the technician hire's timing; and the research data and lab access for serious collaborators.
policy.t2: Detail on the project's batch-variation problem and the unfilled technician post, once there's a real fit.
policy.never: Salary, budget and contract details, family names and private worries, and the grant's financial situation.
